**Kings never see skills** (decided 18 October 2026). A king hears what a character says it can do, and checks it the slow way: a background check, a message to a former employer the character names, his own envoys' reports, rumours. Someone a court has dealt with before arrives with data points attached; a stranger arrives with only his own word. The planned employment-history facts give the checks something to find.

- **Lying about identity.** A stranger may claim to be someone he is not, perhaps borrowing a famous negotiator's name and reputation. Every character has a true identity and a claimed one, and each court's records attach to the name it was given. An impostor is exposed when he meets someone who has seen the real man, or when a check turns up the truth, and both take time. The period's own answer is the one Amenhotep III gave Babylon: send someone who knows the person.

**Seeing oneself (decided 21 October 2026).** Skills belong to characters only; kings have none, and see a character's skills only through his claims and their checks. Now the character does not see his own skills as they are either. Each has a hidden self-assessment: some overestimate themselves, some underestimate, most are roughly right. He sees his skills through it, and the engine uses the true ones, as it always does.

- **What he is told is what he believes.** His request gives his skills as he sees them, as beliefs ("you believe you can slip past any guard"), never as facts, and that belief sits in the part of the request that changes, not in the frozen persona, so it can move.
- **The overconfident** take errands beyond them, claim more when they pitch themselves, ask higher fees and are hired more often, and fail more often when it matters; sometimes boldness carries them anyway, since the dice do not care what anyone believes. **The underconfident** undersell themselves, avoid what they could have done and come cheap: hidden gems for a king who tests people rather than believing them.
- **Claims grow ambiguous in a new way.** A character who overstates himself may not be lying; he may believe it. A king cannot tell a liar from a man deceiving himself ("Kings never see skills").
- **In time he may come to doubt it.** His memory records what happened, plainly, as the engine's facts: the missions that failed, the guards who caught him. A model character reads them and may come to question what he believes about himself, or explain them away, as people do. His self-assessment also moves slowly with what happens to him, and the belief in his request moves with it, so script characters learn too. Outcomes follow his true skill on average, so over many errands he drifts towards the truth, but a run of luck misleads him as it misleads everyone else ("A name made of outcomes"). The inclination never quite goes: the overconfident stay a little overconfident, just as a strategy is where a character starts, not a rule ("The strategy is where he starts, not a rule").
- **It is separate from appetite for risk.** A careful man can still think himself brilliant, and a bold one can know exactly what he can do ("Bold or careful, one goal").

For attested people, the sources sometimes give the inclination. Built with the first character package (build order item 10).

**A name made of outcomes (decided 21 October 2026).** What others know of a character is what they saw happen, never his skill and never his luck. The engine records outcomes as facts (an errand done, gold brought home, a guard slipped past, a capture) and they spread as news and rumour like any other ("Information as a structured asset").

- **Luck makes reputations.** A man who never met an enemy army and whose rolls went his way is spoken of as very able; a skilled man with bad luck is spoken of as a failure. Nobody, the man himself included, can see which was skill and which was chance.
- **A name has a price.** Kings hire by reputation, so a famous name asks a higher fee and gets the errands that matter, which is where luck runs out. A king who tests people ("Kings never see skills") can see past a name; one who trusts rumour pays for it.
- **Rumours bend as they travel.** In the spoken word a tale grows with retelling and ages with distance, so a name abroad may be larger, or older, than the man. A character can also spread tales of his own success, or a rival's failures, which is a claim like any other.
- **The man believes it too.** His own record moves his self-assessment ("Seeing oneself"), so the lucky grow overconfident and the unlucky doubt themselves, each with reason.

Built with the first character package (build order item 10), on the news of item 7.

**Declaring a name** (decided 18 October 2026). The engine can only record a lie it can see, so a name works like gold. When a character first meets a court, by pitching or arriving, it declares a name in a structured field. Its own name is the default; giving another character's name or an invented one is a deliberate choice. The engine knows the truth, so it records the false claim, and an exposed impostor gains a fact such as "posed as Hane at Hattusa". A model character chooses for itself, informed by its persona; a script character follows a formula (dishonest, cunning, or carrying a bad name it wants to escape). A claim made in free text ("I am Pharaoh's interpreter") is only talk, like a spoken offer: kings may believe it or not, but a court's records attach only to the declared name. Text never changes state.

**A past before the game, then a past made in play** (decided 18 October 2026). With no history at the start, every character would be bare traits, the first seasons blank and background checks empty. So characters begin with a few seeded ties standing in for the life they lived before, giving asymmetry from day one. Each must have a mechanical hook, never flavour alone:

- **a sympathy for a court** shapes its choices, as today;
- **a debt** puts pressure on its purse and gives the creditor leverage;
- **a lover or family at a court** draws it there and gives that court a hold over it.

Keep them few. After the start, everything new emerges from play and is recorded only when an engine-visible act happens: skimming, defection, detention, a false name declared and exposed, long years abroad. Lies told in free text are not facts; they stay in the message trail for kings to judge. Greedy and dishonest characters therefore accumulate a past, and checks can find it.

**What servants know** (chosen direction, 18 October 2026). Knowledge is a character's capital. The engine records exactly what passed through each person's hands: every tablet a scribe wrote or read, every mandate an envoy carried, every audience he sat through, every tablet he saw sealed. What a servant knows is therefore a fact, not a guess, and it travels with him, in his memory and as a record the engine can draw on. He knows what he saw and nothing more: a scribe knows his king's tablets, not his troop orders, unless the king told him.

- **Trust and danger grow together.** The longer a scribe or envoy serves, the more he knows and the more a rival would pay for him. The most trusted servant is the largest liability.
- **Leaving is a threat.** A dismissed, unpaid or poached servant takes his master's correspondence with him to the next court; "former employees carry secrets" becomes sharp once scribes exist. A fee due on his return is one way to keep him close.
- **Capture is questioning.** A captured envoy or scribe can be questioned. How much the questioning draws out is an engine roll on his courage and loyalty against the effort spent; what he says is his own decision, and he may lie, which is a choice with a motive like any other. A script character tells the truth or lies by formula from his traits.
- **Knowledge is for sale.** A servant who has left, or who is bribed while still serving, can offer what he knows as a structured report (see "Information as an asset"): a true copy of a tablet he wrote, or a convincing forgery of one he never saw. The buyer cannot easily tell which.
- **Kings learn to compartmentalize.** Keep a secret out of the letter and give it to the envoy by mouth; send different servants to different courts; never let one man see both sides of a double game. Each choice trades convenience against exposure, which is real statecraft and needs no rule.
- **Silencing has a price.** Executing a man because he knows too much travels as a rumour, by the same carriers as any other, and a court known for it finds hiring harder, as with executions of liars.

Nothing here needs a new system: it follows from what the engine already records, characters' memory and facts, rumours that need carriers, and characters deciding for themselves. What it needs is the engine's record of who saw what, and questioning as a captive order.

**What skills cover** (decided 18 October 2026). Personality, not skill, decides the urge to alter a message: a model character chooses for itself, informed by its persona, and a script character follows a formula on its traits. Skills cover what the engine decides, and few belong to one profession; all shape what a character picks up and escapes on the road:

- gathering information (what an envoy or spy notices, and how accurately);
- avoiding detection and capture;
- spotting forgeries, including assaying gold: an assay is done by one of the court's people, and a poor assayer may miss a good alloy or wrongly accuse honest gold;
- making forgeries, including debasing gold: the king decides whether to cheat and how far, and the worker's skill decides how well the alloy passes inspection (gold changed hands by weight, so cheating meant alloying it with silver or copper; Babylon complained of Egyptian gold that looked like silver);
- commanding armies (the size of a commander's tactical search);
- languages, a skill of 0–100 in each, and an aptitude for learning them (see "Languages" below).

**Languages** (decided 19 October 2026, replacing the relay chain of 18 October). The game keeps one mediator between two kings, the envoy, because he is the one with a motive to bend a message, and because one mediator keeps the message trail readable: what the king wrote, what the envoy said abroad, what the host answered and what the envoy reported home ("The message trail" in the main tab). His choice costs output only when he makes it: he passes his king's words on as written, or reports an answer as given, with a flag, the engine copies the text, and only what he changes or adds is written out ("Output is the other half" in the main tab). A chain of scribes and interpreters, each rolling for loss and each deciding how faithful to be, was dropped: it added many steps that could go wrong, was hard to balance, cost several model calls a round trip, buried the envoy's choices in noise, and gave the extra mediators almost no reason to lie.

**Language skill buys time, never noise.** Like every other skill, a character's skill in each language is a hidden number from 0 to 100, never shown to players. When something has to cross a language, whoever does the crossing sets the chance that it succeeds this season, rolled each season until it does: from about 80 it succeeds at once; below that, the chance each season is roughly the skill as a percentage; at 0 it never does, until someone learns. Where two people are involved, the weaker skill counts. Nothing is garbled; a weak speaker is slow. In words, for a character's persona, its claims and the narrator, the number reads as none, halting, good or fluent: a model character knows its Hittite is "good", and may boast that it is fluent.

- **Speaking.** The envoy is understood when he and someone at the host's court, the king or any servant, share a language; the chance comes from the poorer of the two in their best shared language, any language counting, a court's or not. A servant who bridges passes the envoy's words on faithfully, since he has nothing to gain by changing them, unless he is in someone else's pay ("A go-between for hire"). The same rule holds between any two characters in the same place: each season they try, and once they understand each other the whole message passes, never garbled ("Characters deal with each other"; decided 21 October 2026). The dice fall first (decided 21 October 2026): at the start of each season, before any model is called, the engine settles who understands whom, for every pair of characters in the same place and every envoy at a court, and each character's request says whom he can make himself understood to this season. He writes only to them, so no call is spent on words nobody will understand, and one who badly wants to talk to someone waits and tries again next season. When nobody at a court understands an envoy, the king is told so plainly (below), and the envoy's model is never asked to speak.
- **A go-between for hire (decided 21 October 2026).** Two characters with no shared language can hire a third who speaks both to bridge for them, on a job like any other ("Jobs, not wages" in the main tab), and a court can hire one for an envoy nobody there understands. He can also post a standing price where he lives, for each pair of languages he bridges, and anyone there may use him at that price without bargaining, paying him for each message he carries across; a script go-between sets his price by expected income, as for any fee ("Fees clear the market"). The dice that settle who understands whom count him in ("Speaking"), so a character's request lists whom he can reach through a go-between and at what price, and no call is spent on haggling. Each side is understood through him by the same chance, from the weakest skill along the way. So a man with several languages at a busy door, Ugarit or Alashiya's port where strangers land, can live on it ("Working for oneself"), as interpreters did: Akkadian already had a word for him, targumannu, the root of "dragoman". He follows the scribe's rule ("A king seals what his scribe wrote"), as a bridging court servant does. An ordinary go-between passes the words on faithfully, since he has no motive to do otherwise, and the engine relays them with no model call. One in someone else's pay, bribed by the other side or by a third party, may bend what he passes on, softening a threat, inflating an offer or dropping a condition; only then is his model called, once for each message he bridges, so honesty costs nothing and only a real betrayal costs a call. The pay is a fact the engine holds, a motive with a name on it: he is in someone else's pay when the engine holds a job, or gold handed to him, from anyone other than whoever pays him for this exchange (for a court servant, anyone other than his own king), given within the past year or still in force. Anyone present who understands both languages may notice the difference, by the same chance as in "Speaking", and it becomes something he knows and can sell or tell ("What servants know"); otherwise the victim learns only when the consequences come back. Either way the go-between hears every word, so, like the scribe, he can be bribed, questioned or spied on, and can sell what he heard.
- **An envoy not yet understood chooses** whether to stay until he is, go home, or lie and report that his message was delivered. Lying saves time, and his king may not learn the truth for a year; the choice has a motive, and it is his. While he stays, he learns.
- **Where nobody at court shares any language with him,** the king is told so plainly ("nobody at your court understands him; he presented gifts weighing 40 shekels"), never shown gibberish, which a model would try to decode. Gifts are then the only language until someone learns, and the easiest thing for an envoy to steal from.
- **Reading a tablet.** The king chooses who translates it, and the chance comes from the translator's weaker skill of the two languages concerned, the tablet's and the king's. An unreadable tablet waits until a reader is found (see "Tablets are objects in a place"); an urgent one is a reason to hire a better reader.
- **Composing.** A king speaks his own language, so his envoy must grasp it. A native servant does so at once; a foreign hire with halting Egyptian needs longer to take in his mandate and leaves later, unless someone at court bridges for him. A tablet in a foreign language needs a scribe who writes it, and a weaker scribe takes longer.
- **Learning by living there.** Each season a character lives in a province, his skill rises in the languages spoken there, and only in those ("Where each language is spoken"; decided 21 October 2026), quickly at first and slowly near the top. How fast depends on a hidden aptitude for languages, from 0 to 100 like every skill; on how widely each language is spoken there; and on the share of the season he spent in the province, the same accounting as the road check, so a resident learns a full season's worth and a traveller passing through almost none. Nobody learns from the company he keeps: standing next to a Hittite teaches nothing. Detained envoys come home speaking their hosts' tongue, and a king can send a young servant to Hattusa only to learn Hittite, a better bet if the servant is quick. Aptitude is hidden like every skill: a character may claim to learn quickly, and only time tells. It is more common among scribes and merchants, who live by words.
- **"Alien" courts.** Where no language overlaps, two courts talk through a proxy court that understands both, invest years in learning, or exchange only gifts.

**Who speaks what.** Characters start with the languages of where they come from: their home court's language fluently, and Akkadian at a skill that depends on their background, highest for scribes, merchants and former envoys. People from trading cities like Ugarit may speak several. Arrivals during play take their languages from their origin in the same way. For a stranger from beyond the map, his reason for coming sets how much he knows of a map language and his door sets which (decided 21 October 2026): a trader or a soldier for hire who has come this way before has some of the language spoken where his door opens, broken Akkadian at Ugarit, some Luwian on Arzawa's coast, some Akkadian on the eastern road and the Gulf; a wanderer, a refugee or a man from the tin lands has none; and a local coming home is fluent in his own ("Arrivals come through doors"). His own tongue still counts, since any language two characters share lets them talk ("Speaking"). Kings and rulers follow the same rules: a king speaks his own court's language and whatever the sources give him, learns by living somewhere like anyone, and otherwise talks through a go-between, as Tushratta dictated in Hurrian and sealed letters written in Akkadian. A servant who speaks Akkadian and a rare court language, such as Hittite, well is valuable. A character knows its own skills, in words, so it seeks work where they are worth most and prices itself accordingly; kings hear only its claims, and only results show whether "I speak Hittite well" was true (see "Kings never see skills").

**The court languages.** About five, not seven: Egyptian, Hittite, Hurrian (Mitanni), Luwian (Arzawa) and Akkadian, which Babylonia and Assyria speak natively in their own dialects. Alashiya's own language is unknown (undeciphered in reality), and its letters are in Akkadian. Babylonian and Assyrian envoys need no second language for diplomacy, which is Babylon's cultural prestige in mechanical form and belongs on the balance checklist. Arzawa is the period's example of a court outside the Akkadian world: its two letters in the archive (EA 31 and 32) are in Hittite, the reply asks Egypt to keep writing in Hittite, and these two tablets are what first showed, in 1902, that Hittite is an Indo-European language. Which courts read which languages is map data.

**Where each language is spoken (decided 21 October 2026).** Which languages are spoken in each province, and how widely, is map data from the history pass. Everywhere there is the people's own tongue: Canaanite in the Levantine cities, whose scribes glossed their Akkadian letters with words of their own speech; Ugaritic at Ugarit; a Nubian tongue in Nubia; Luwian in Arzawa's lands; Hurrian across Mitanni. A court adds its own language, and Akkadian where it keeps Akkadian scribes. So the people's tongues are languages like any other, not only the five court languages above: two Levantine characters understand each other in Canaanite, and a newcomer at Ugarit can pick up the street's Ugaritic before the scribes' Akkadian. A character learns only what is spoken where he lives ("Learning by living there"), and which languages a court reads in its tablets stays a separate fact ("Reading a tablet").

**Calibration.** In the period nearly every great court kept Akkadian scribes, so if Akkadian is common, languages will rarely block anything. The interesting cases come from making it scarcer at the edges, perhaps at Arzawa or Alashiya; that is tuned from games. Arrivals already lean that way, since the western sea brings Aegeans with no Akkadian to exactly those coasts ("Arrivals come through doors").

**A lingua franca by incentive, not by rule.** Nothing makes Akkadian the language of diplomacy. A court is understood only where it shares a language, so courts drift toward whatever tongue the most servants speak, and Akkadian, spoken most widely, is the obvious candidate. If another language spread instead, through hiring or arrivals, the drift would follow it.

**Language is also how one hears.** What a character picks up at a foreign court, its gossip, rumours and careless talk, depends on its information-gathering skill and on how well it speaks that court's own language. An envoy who speaks Hittite well at Hattusa overhears what one speaking only Akkadian never will, which gives every language a value beyond carrying letters.
